solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Blokes answer with crude empty threat

parts.note: blokes are men

indicators.note: an empty word has its insides removed, leaving only the outer letters of crude

explanation.surface: Some men respond with a coarse but hollow threat.
explanation.definitionFit: A menace is a danger or an implied warning of harm, so it is a synonym for threat.

clue.text: Exhaust section of staff and I go bankrupt

parts.note: to staff a post is to man it
a business that folds goes bankrupt

explanation.surface: Part of a car's exhaust, or a firm's staff and boss going bust.
explanation.definitionFit: A manifold is the pipe assembly gathering a car engine's exhaust gases, part of the exhaust system.

clue.text: Is suspect following drug agent's plant

indicators.note: following puts the words before it after the word for drug agent

parts.note: a narc is a US narcotics agent; the 's means is, linking to the definition
sus is slang for suspect or suspicious

explanation.surface: An informer's plant is suspicious, following a drug officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' looks like a spy or planted evidence, but it is a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Narcissus is a genus of bulb plants including daffodils.

clue.text: Islander's arrest oddly ignored in nick

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, so the definition is just islander

indicators.note: in means the kept letters go inside the prison word

parts.note: nick is British slang for prison, as is can

indicators.note: oddly ignored means the odd letters of arrest are dropped, keeping the even ones

explanation.surface: An islander is caught, though oddly the arrest is overlooked at the police station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nick' means both arrest and prison in British slang; here it is prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cretan is a native of Crete, the largest Greek island, so an islander.

clue.text: Left inside, began to get frightened

indicators.note: inside tells us the letter for left goes within the word for began

parts.note: began means started

explanation.surface: Someone who stayed behind slowly starts to feel scared.
explanation.definitionFit: Startled means alarmed by something sudden, a near synonym for frightened.

clue.text: I'd worry after confusing cracking tune with 14

definitions.note: 14 points to the clue at 14 across, a light comic stage work

indicators.note: cracking means breaking into, so the jumbled letters burst into the other pieces

parts.note: a theme is a melody or tune

indicators.note: confusing means mixing up, so the letters of I'd worry are jumbled

explanation.surface: A worried composer fears that muddling a tune will spoil a light opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' gives W, a common abbreviation; 'cracking' has the jumbled letters break into the tune-plus-W pair just before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Merry Widow is Lehár's 1905 operetta, so it is an example of the light musical form at 14.

clue.text: Go back and buy another round?

definitions.meaning: to treat the company to drinks again

explanation.surface: Drinkers at the bar wonder whether to head home or order more.
explanation.definitionFit: Retreat means withdraw, while re-treat playfully means stand drinks a second time.

clue.text: Riches entice boxing champions at first

indicators.note: boxing means enclosing, so the word for tempt surrounds the letter

parts.note: to entice is to lure

indicators.note: at first takes the opening letter of champions

explanation.surface: The money in prize fights attracts top boxers.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucre is money or profit, often filthy lucre, so it means riches.

clue.text: Thin detective picked up stolen goods

parts.note: DI is a Detective Inspector

indicators.note: picked up as by a microphone: the word for plunder is heard, not seen

parts.note: stolen goods are loot

explanation.surface: A skinny detective has recovered stolen property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thin' looks like an adjective for the detective; it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To dilute a liquid is to weaken or thin it by adding water.

clue.text: Brass section in Wagner vexes

indicators.note: section in says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An orchestra's brass players are annoyed by some Wagner, famous for heavy brass writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Brass is informal for cheek or audacity, as is nerve: 'he had the brass neck to ask'.

clue.text: One in charge of feeding of canines? The very same

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: feeding here means going into, so the in-charge letters are fed into the word for teeth

parts.note: canines are teeth, so something of canines is dental

explanation.surface: Asks who looks after feeding the dogs, then answers that it is the same person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'canines' suggests dogs, but here it means teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Identical means exactly alike, the very same thing in every respect.

clue.text: Largely unskilled, could be niece described primarily as this?

definitions.text: Largely unskilled, could be niece described primarily as this?

indicators.note: largely means most but not all, so the word for unskilled loses its last letter

parts.note: unskilled means inexpert

indicators.note: could be says the letters of niece can be rearranged
primarily takes the first letter of described

explanation.surface: Asks whether a young, unskilled niece would be described this way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' signals rearranging the letters of niece. The whole clue doubles as the definition: someone largely unskilled.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking experience means largely unskilled, as a young niece might be.

clue.text: Lot appointed to acquire sails etc for ship

indicators.note: to acquire means the word for destiny takes in the other piece

parts.note: one's appointed lot in life is one's fate
a ship's rig is its sails, masts and so on

explanation.surface: A group of people is assigned to buy sails and other gear for a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lot' looks like a batch of goods or people; it is one's destiny.
explanation.definitionFit: A frigate is a type of warship, so it is an example of a ship.

clue.text: Ecstasy and cocaine ignored by lenient copper?

parts.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy

indicators.note: ignored by means the drug letter is left out of the word for merciful

parts.note: lenient means clement, merciful
C is slang shorthand for cocaine

explanation.surface: A soft-hearted policeman turns a blind eye to drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' is a policeman in the surface; the question mark flags that it is an example of a chemical substance.
explanation.definitionFit: Copper is a chemical element, so the definition is an example, as the question mark signals.

clue.text: Table that shows change to make laser into taser?

definitions.text: Table that shows change to make laser into taser?

parts.words: Table that shows change to make laser into taser?
parts.note: a table of items, whose name, split into letters and a short verb, states the single swap that turns laser into taser: its first letter becomes a T

explanation.surface: Asks for a chart showing how one stun weapon turns into another.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping laser's first letter for a T gives taser; write that swap as 'letter equals letter' and the word for a table appears.
explanation.definitionFit: A table is an arranged set of items, and a list is the same sort of tabulated record.

clue.text: Harry Potter, a tale ultimately for light entertainment

indicators.note: to harry is to harass or worry, so these letters are disturbed into a new order
ultimately points to the final letter of tale

explanation.surface: A Harry Potter story is ultimately just fun reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' looks like the boy wizard's name, but to harry is to harass, and here it signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: An operetta is a short, light comic opera, a staged form of light entertainment.

clue.text: A puzzle setter is given books as surprise

parts.note: a maze is a puzzle of paths
the setter refers to himself as me
NT is the New Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A crossword compiler handed some books is astonished.
explanation.definitionFit: Amazement is great wonder at something unexpected, a strong form of surprise.

clue.text: The early shifts? That'll be tough

indicators.note: shifts means moves around, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Working early shifts is hard going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shifts' looks like work rotas, but it signals rearranging THE EARLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Leathery means tough and hard like leather, as with overcooked meat.

clue.text: Boom and bust worse mostly for singers

parts.note: a boom is a spar on a ship's mast

indicators.note: bust means broken, so the letters left are jumbled
mostly means the word worse loses its final letter

explanation.surface: An economic cycle of boom and bust is bad news for musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bust' rearranges WORS (from 'worse mostly') into ROWS.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparrows are small birds noted for chirping, so they are singers in the songbird sense.

clue.text: Increase number in police force after a month

indicators.note: after places the police piece after the month

parts.note: Aug is short for August

indicators.note: in means the letter for number sits within the police abbreviation

parts.note: the Met is London's Metropolitan Police

explanation.surface: More officers are added to the police after a month.
explanation.walkthrough: THE MET is London's Metropolitan Police.
explanation.definitionFit: To augment is to enlarge or add to, so it is a synonym of increase.

clue.text: Look out — could be a pothole!

definitions.meaning: a schoolboy's Latin warning shout, beware, as lookouts used at public schools
a pothole in the caving sense is a deep natural shaft or cavern, one example of an underground hollow

explanation.surface: A warning shout to someone about to step into a hole in the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pothole' suggests a hole in the road, but it is the caver's sense. 'Look out' is Latin cave, beware, once a British schoolboy's warning.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin imperative beware was shouted as a warning; a pothole is a vertical cavern, a kind of underground chamber.

clue.text: She possibly entertains one in centre of Tagawa?

definitions.text: She possibly entertains one in centre of Tagawa?

indicators.note: in means the rest goes inside those middle letters
centre of takes the middle two letters of Tagawa
entertains means takes in as a guest, so the jumbled letters hold the numeral
possibly says the letters of she may be arranged another way

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A Japanese hostess entertains a guest in the middle of Tagawa, a city in Japan.
explanation.walkthrough: Tagawa is a real Japanese city, chosen so its middle letters can hold the rest. The whole clue describes what a geisha does.
explanation.definitionFit: A geisha is a Japanese woman trained to entertain guests, which is what the whole clue describes.

clue.text: With Jack gone, push Rex to be groom

indicators.note: gone means the card letter is removed

parts.note: to jostle is to push and shove
J is the card abbreviation for jack
R stands for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Jack has left, so someone pushes Rex to marry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'groom' suggests a bridegroom, but it is a stable hand.
explanation.definitionFit: An ostler is a stableman at an inn who looks after horses, so a groom in the horse sense.

clue.text: Poem regularly perused? That's entertaining stuff

indicators.note: entertaining in the sense of hosting: the alternate letters take in the word for block
regularly picks every other letter of perused

parts.note: to stuff or block something is to clog it

explanation.surface: Wonders whether a poem read at intervals counts as amusing material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' gives EUE, the even letters of perused, which hold CLOG.
explanation.definitionFit: An eclogue is a short pastoral poem, often a dialogue between shepherds, as in Virgil.

clue.text: Permissible to tout? Not so

indicators.note: not here strips away the following word from the verb for tout

parts.note: to tout for business is to solicit

explanation.surface: Is it allowed to sell tickets on the street? Apparently not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not so' reads as a denial; it says remove SO from SOLICIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Licit means lawful or allowed, the opposite of illicit, so permissible.

clue.text: Heading off, worried about fool?

indicators.note: about means the remaining letters are turned round
heading off means the first letter of the word for anxious is dropped

parts.note: worried means stressed

explanation.surface: Someone sets off anxious about having been taken for an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns TRESSED round after 'Heading off' removes the first S of STRESSED. A fool is a British pudding of fruit and cream.
explanation.definitionFit: A fool is a pudding of puréed fruit and cream, so it is an example of a sweet course; hence the question mark.

clue.text: Scored runs, securing a century before wicket — it's above criticism

indicators.note: before places the cricket letter after the rest
securing means holding: the shuffled letters close round the other pieces
runs as in a colour running: the letters of scored spread into a new order

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a century
W is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a wicket

explanation.surface: A cricket report: a batter scored runs, reaching a hundred before losing a wicket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'runs' rearranges SCORED round A and C to give SACREDCO; 'before' puts W last. Runs, century and wicket all look like cricket terms.
explanation.definitionFit: A sacred cow is an idea or institution treated as beyond question, immune from criticism.

clue.text: For example, interrupting to press subject

indicators.note: interrupting means breaking into, so the example abbreviation goes inside the other word

parts.note: to lie heavy on something is to press down on it

explanation.surface: Someone cuts in, for instance, to push a point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'subject' looks like a topic, but it is a person owing allegiance.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers gives subject as a sense of liege: a vassal bound to a feudal lord.

clue.text: Position needs Penny for the first time to show skill

indicators.note: read as 'for the first T': the penny letter replaces the first T

parts.note: an attitude is a bodily position or posture

explanation.surface: A first attempt shows that a stance needs some money to show talent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for the first time' reads as 'for the first T', so P replaces the first T of ATTITUDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Aptitude is a natural talent or ability, close in meaning to skill.

clue.text: Rather small-minded? About right

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for mean-spirited goes round the letter

parts.note: small-minded means petty

explanation.surface: Asks whether someone is being a bit narrow-minded, then agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rather' sounds like an answer, but it is the definition, as in 'pretty good'.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adverb, pretty means fairly or somewhat, as in 'pretty good', a synonym of rather.
